name: Treaty with the New York Indians, 1838 (Treaty of Buffalo Creek)
promises: In return for the New York Indians' lands at Green Bay, Wisconsin (except one tract), the United States would set apart 1,824,000 acres west of Missouri (in what became Kansas) as a permanent home for all the New York Indians (Articles 1 and 2).
The United States would appropriate $400,000 to help the Indians remove, support themselves the first year after removal, and for education, farming, mills, animals and tools (Article 15).

Article 10 recorded that the Seneca had sold their remaining New York reservations by deed to Thomas Ludlow Ogden and Joseph Fellows for $202,000, in the presence and with the approval of the US commissioner, and the United States assented to the sale.
Separate articles covered the Tuscarora, who conveyed 5,000 acres to the United States in trust and had a deed to Ogden and Fellows approved.

breaches.what: The Supreme Court found that after the treaty the United States surveyed the Kansas lands promised as a permanent home, made them public domain and sold them, keeping the proceeds. It rejected the argument that the Indians forfeited the land by not removing, reversed the Court of Claims, and ordered judgment for the net amount the government received for the Kansas lands.

landTaken: The Kansas tract promised by Article 2 contained 1,824,000 acres (New York Indians v. United States, 1898).
compensation: The 1898 Supreme Court ordered judgment for the net amount the United States actually received for the Kansas lands, without interest, less the share settled with the Tonawanda Band (who had relinquished their Kansas interest for $256,000 under the 1857 treaty) and other deductions. The final dollar figure of that judgment was not confirmed here.
today: The Seneca deed in this treaty was replaced by the 1842 compromise, under which the Seneca Nation kept Allegany and Cattaraugus and lost Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda; the Tonawanda Band later repurchased part of its land under the 1857 treaty.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's archive calls the 1838 Buffalo Creek treaty fraudulently executed.

openQuestions: The final amount paid under the 1898 judgment, and when, was not confirmed.

The Indian Claims Commission did not separately value the 1838 Seneca deed: in Dockets 342-A and 368-A the Court of Claims and Commission treated the 1842 compromise, not 1838, as the operative sale (Commission, 1972).

The circumstances of signing (bribery and alcohol alleged by contemporaries and the Society of Friends, and the Senate's amendment and re-submission before proclamation) were not documented from a primary source in this pass.

Audit 2026-11-08: promise on Article 15 rewritten from the treaty text ($400,000 for removal, first-year support, education, farming and mills) instead of the Supreme Court's paraphrase; the Seneca deed promise now cites Article 10, where the $202,000 deed appears.
